ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Roald Amundsen — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for cold-induced burning pain and numbness in the fingers of both hands: history, examination, blood tests for other causes of neuropathy, mood screening, cold protection, and a neurology referral

text.paragraph: New patient visit for cold-induced burning pain and numbness in the fingers of both hands: history, examination, blood tests for other causes of neuropathy, mood screening, cold protection, and a neurology referral [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: The pain and clumsiness in his fingers in the cold make him fear he can no longer work in the Arctic. [S]
He does not want any medicine that makes him drowsy, because he drives and flies. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on July 16, 1872, at the farm Hvidtsten in Borge, Østfold, Norway. [D]

He wrote that as a young man he was near-sighted, a defect that had gradually improved but was not wholly corrected, and that he had refused to wear the glasses prescribed for him so that it would not keep him out of military training. [D]

On a winter ski crossing of the Hardangervidda plateau in his early twenties he nearly died in a snow cave during a rest stop, and he wrote that he and his companion both got their fingers badly frostbitten while breaking into a nailed-up hut. [D]

As first mate of the Belgian Antarctic expedition in the Belgica (1897 to 1899), he spent thirteen months in the pack ice. He wrote that every member of the ship's company was afflicted with scurvy and all but three were prostrated by it; once fresh seal and penguin meat was eaten, the men plainly improved within a week. The expedition's physician had encouraged the crew to eat seal and penguin. [D]

A physician historian argues that the heart failure seen on the Belgica expedition, described at the time as 'polar anaemia', was almost certainly wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency, and that most sufferers were probably also deficient in vitamin C. [R]

He led the first voyage through the Northwest Passage in a single ship, the Gjøa (1903 to 1906), and on December 14, 1911, he and four companions were the first to reach the South Pole. In 1925 he led a flight by flying boat toward the North Pole from Ny-Ålesund, and in 1926 the flight of the airship Norge across the Arctic. [D]

On the Maud expedition, in the autumn of 1918, he fell down the ship's runway onto his right shoulder; the fracture was set aboard by a crewman trained in first aid, and he kept to his bed for eight days. On November 8, 1918, a polar bear struck him on the back, leaving minor gashes. He wrote that he could not at first lift his right hand to use a pencil, worked the arm daily for months, and that a surgeon in Seattle who X-rayed it in 1921 found the shoulder in a condition that theoretically would make the arm unusable. [D]

About the New Year of 1918 to 1919, working in the small, unventilated observatory of the Maud with a kerosene vapour lamp, he became drowsy, felt his heart beating unnaturally, and nearly lost consciousness before he reached fresh air. He wrote that the violent palpitation lasted several days, that for months strenuous exercise set his heart pounding, and that in February he was exhausted by climbing a fifty-foot hill. [D]

He wrote that in February 1922 a heart specialist in London told him "No more expeditions!" and to avoid all strenuous exercise; nine months later he travelled about 800 miles on foot through the snow from Point Barrow to Nome, and five years later he wrote that he had had no unpleasant results from his exertions. [D]
The Norwegian encyclopedia describes the observatory episode as carbon monoxide poisoning. [R]

He bought the house Uranienborg at Svartskog, on the Bunnefjord near Oslo, in 1908 and lived there for twenty years. His study had an exercise spring installed in the floor for his strength training, and a pump brought salt water from the fjord for his morning bath. [D]
After his 1927 lecture tour of Japan he returned by the Trans-Siberian railway; letters place him in Oslo in August 1927 and again in May 1928. [D]

The Norwegian encyclopedia writes that by the end of his career he felt tired, lonely and bitter; he was 55, with persistent money problems and no more poles to conquer. He had declared himself personally bankrupt. [D]

text.paragraph: 3 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Near-sightedness since youth, partly improved, never fully corrected
Frostbite of the fingers of both hands on a winter ski crossing in his early twenties
Scurvy during thirteen months in the Antarctic pack ice in his mid-twenties, with recovery on fresh seal and penguin meat

Complicated fracture of the right upper arm in a fall on board ship in his mid-forties, set without surgery, with months of self-directed rehabilitation; minor back wounds from a polar bear the same autumn

Near-collapse with palpitations from lamp fumes in a closed observatory, with months of exertional palpitations and a slow recovery; later advised by a heart specialist to give up expeditions, without lasting effect on his exercise tolerance by his account

list.item: Polar explorer and expedition leader, now writing and lecturing; still plans flights and expeditions in the Arctic; often travels by air and sea [S]
Lives in his own house on a fjord outside Oslo; under financial strain after a bankruptcy [S]
Exercise: strength training with floor springs most mornings, a cold salt-water bath each morning, and long walks and skiing; no limitation [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: rarely, a glass of wine at a dinner; no other drugs [S]
Drives a car and flies as a passenger and expedition navigator; wants to stay fit to fly in the Arctic [S]

text.paragraph: No medications started by this date.

Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, courteous and guarded; tired and worried about money; PHQ-9 score 5. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

list.item: Burning pain, numbness and tingling in the fingers of both hands, brought on by cold for many winters and worse this winter, with the fingers turning white then blue then red in the cold; average pain 6 of 10; cause not yet established at intake; nerve conduction studies and neurology consultation requested: active, confirmed [S]

Old fracture of the upper end of the right humerus, set at sea and rehabilitated without surgery: forward flexion and abduction limited to about 120 degrees, without pain at rest: active, confirmed [S]

Neurology consultation in two weeks with nerve conduction studies to confirm or exclude a late post-frostbite neuropathy, entrapment, or another polyneuropathy, and to advise on treatment that does not cause drowsiness. Guideline: Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings (CG173) (2013, updated 2020); Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Frostbite: 2024 Update (McIntosh SE, et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2024;35(2):183-197) (2024) [S]

Cold protection and hand care: liner gloves under mittens, heated gloves and hand warmers outdoors, warming the hands before fine work, no cold-water hand washing, and checking the fingers for skin damage. Guideline: Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Frostbite: 2024 Update (McIntosh SE, et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2024;35(2):183-197) (2024) [S]

Blood tests for other causes of neuropathy: glucose and HbA1c, vitamin B12, TSH, kidney function, liver enzyme and hemoglobin; PHQ-9 for mood with chronic pain. Guideline: Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings (CG173) (2013, updated 2020); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
Referral to neurology (peripheral nerve), Henrik Abernathy-Dahl, MD, ordered 1928-02-10 [S]
